```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo    = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE
)

library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(tidyr)
library(scales)

data_dir    <- "delta-calibration-data"
t1_dir      <- file.path(data_dir, "type-1-error")
t1_meff_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "type-1-error", "meff_gt_5")
pow_dir     <- file.path(data_dir, "power")

t1_stat      <- read_csv(file.path(t1_dir,      "summary_by_stat.csv"),         show_col_types = FALSE)
t1_meffbin   <- read_csv(file.path(t1_dir,      "summary_by_stat_meffbin.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
t1m_stat     <- read_csv(file.path(t1_meff_dir, "summary_by_stat.csv"),         show_col_types = FALSE)
t1m_meffbin  <- read_csv(file.path(t1_meff_dir, "summary_by_stat_meffbin.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
pow_summary  <- read_csv(file.path(pow_dir,     "power_summary.csv"),           show_col_types = FALSE)
tmpl_effects <- read_csv(file.path(pow_dir,     "template_effects.csv"),        show_col_types = FALSE)
n80          <- read_csv(file.path(pow_dir,     "n_for_80pct_power.csv"),       show_col_types = FALSE)

ALPHA  <- 0.05
N_SIM  <- 300L
B_PERM <- 150000L

stat_labels <- c(af = "AF", cct = "CCT", maxmean = "Maxmean", stouffer = "Stouffer")
stat_order  <- c("stouffer", "af", "maxmean", "cct")
```

# Introduction

## Background and Motivation

This document reports the results of a simulation study designed to evaluate
how well different statistical aggregation methods perform when used within
`compute_delta` — a test for detecting differences in antibody responses between
two groups of subjects, based on phage-display immunoprecipitation sequencing
(PhIP-Seq) data.

In PhIP-Seq experiments, a patient's serum is incubated with a library of
bacteriophages, each displaying a short peptide sequence. Peptides recognised
by antibodies are enriched and sequenced. The result is a high-dimensional
binary matrix: for each subject and each peptide, we observe either a "hit" (1)
or no binding (0). Individual peptide hits are then aggregated to the level of
a taxonomic feature of interest (e.g. a viral species), and the question is
whether the distribution of aggregated hits differs between two groups.

`compute_delta` performs this group comparison by (i) computing a per-peptide
test statistic, (ii) aggregating these statistics across all peptides mapping to
a given feature, and (iii) assessing significance via a permutation test. This
study evaluates four aggregation strategies:

- **Stouffer's method** — combines standardised scores linearly, weighting each
  peptide equally. Benefits from diffuse signal across many peptides.
- **AF (Aggregate Function)** — an adaptive combination method that adjusts
  weighting based on the data.
- **Maxmean** — uses the mean of the most extreme (positive or negative) subset
  of scores. Designed to detect concentrated effects driven by a few peptides.
- **Cauchy Combination Test (CCT)** — combines p-values via a weighted Cauchy
  transformation, intended to be robust to correlation structure.

> **Important note on CCT.** Preliminary screening showed that CCT is
> essentially non-functional in this setting — it reaches 80% power in only 1
> out of 156 simulation scenarios. Its type-1 error rate also grows above the
> nominal level as the number of effective peptides increases, reaching 11.7%
> at features with 250–500 effective peptides. The root cause is structural:
> CCT was designed for a small number of independent or weakly dependent
> p-values, whereas in PhIP-Seq data, peptides mapping to the same taxon are
> highly correlated. For these reasons, CCT is retained in the type-1 error
> results for completeness but excluded from the power discussion.

## Study Design: Anchor Samples and the Null Distribution

A fundamental challenge in calibration evaluation is obtaining a dataset where
the null hypothesis is genuinely true. To solve this, we used **anchor
samples**: the serum of 12 patients was pooled into a single mixture and
measured repeatedly across multiple independent runs and plates. Because all
measurements come from the exact same biological material, any observed
differences between measurements can only arise from technical noise — there is
no biological signal by definition.

A critical subtlety is that measurements from the same run are expected to be
more similar to each other than measurements from different runs. To prevent
this from inflating apparent significance, all permutations were **stratified
by run**: observations were only permuted within the same run.

## Simulation Overview

**Type-1 error evaluation** was performed by running `compute_delta` on the
anchor data across 30 independent permutation iterations. In each iteration,
subjects were randomly assigned to two artificial groups and p-values computed
for every taxon. Any p-value below α = 0.05 constitutes a false positive.

**Power evaluation** used synthetic data constructed from six **effect
templates** — empirically-derived peptide-level prevalence profiles from real
biological comparisons. The simulation grid covered:

- `r length(unique(pow_summary$n_per_group))` sample sizes:
  `r paste(sort(unique(pow_summary$n_per_group)), collapse = ", ")` subjects
  per group
- `r length(unique(pow_summary$n_peptides_cfg))` peptide counts:
  `r paste(sort(unique(pow_summary$n_peptides_cfg)), collapse = ", ")`
- `r N_SIM` simulations per cell | `r format(B_PERM, big.mark = ",")` permutations per test

---

# Type-1 Error Analysis

## Overall Calibration

The calibration plot below shows, for each aggregation method, how closely the
observed false-positive rate tracks the nominal significance threshold across
the full range of α values. A perfectly calibrated test follows the diagonal;
points below the diagonal indicate conservative behaviour.

```{r fig-calib-all, fig.cap="Calibration plot across all features. A well-calibrated test follows the dashed diagonal. All methods are conservative.", out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(t1_dir, "calibration_plot.png"))
```

All four methods are conservative — the observed false-positive rates are
substantially below the nominal level. Table 1 summarises the empirical rates
averaged over `r nrow(t1_stat %>% filter(aggregate_stat_used == "af"))` iterations.

```{r tab-t1-all}
t1_stat %>%
  mutate(
    Method            = stat_labels[aggregate_stat_used],
    `Type-1 (α=0.05)` = sprintf("%.1f%%", mean_type1_0.05 * 100),
    `Type-1 (α=0.01)` = sprintf("%.1f%%", mean_type1_0.01 * 100),
    `λ_GC`            = sprintf("%.2f",   mean_lambda_gc)
  ) %>%
  arrange(match(aggregate_stat_used, stat_order)) %>%
  select(Method, `Type-1 (α=0.05)`, `Type-1 (α=0.01)`, `λ_GC`) %>%
  kable(
    align   = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
    caption = "Empirical type-1 error rates and genomic inflation factor (λ_GC) across all features. Nominal levels: 5% and 1%."
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

The **genomic inflation factor** (λ_GC) measures the median observed test
statistic relative to what is expected under the null. A value of 1.0 is ideal.
In a permutation test, inflated test statistics do not automatically lead to
inflated p-values — the p-value is computed against the permutation
distribution, which is similarly inflated. The conservative p-values here
confirm this.

## Consistency Across Iterations

```{r fig-t1-iter, fig.cap="Type-1 error rate per iteration (30 runs) for each aggregation method. The red dashed line marks the nominal 5% threshold.", out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(t1_dir, "type1_rate_by_iter.png"))
```

All methods remain consistently below the 5% threshold in every iteration,
confirming robust control across the full range of anchor measurements.

## Effect of Feature Complexity: The m_eff Problem

The conservatism above is strongly driven by a large number of features with
very few effective peptides (m_eff). The **effective number of peptides**
(m_eff) accounts for correlation between overlapping or similar sequences.
Features with m_eff = 1 or 2 carry almost no aggregated information: the
permutation p-value simply cannot be very small because there are too few
distinct configurations to permute.

```{r fig-phist-meff, fig.cap="Histogram of observed p-values stratified by m_eff bin. Features with m_eff ≤ 5 show a strongly right-skewed distribution consistent with severe conservatism.", out.width="95%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(t1_dir, "p_hist_by_stat_meff.png"))
```

Features with m_eff ≤ 5 show a massive spike at p = 1 — they almost never
reach significance. This is an artefact of the discrete permutation test, not
a biological signal, and it pulls the overall type-1 error rate far below the
nominal level.

**For this reason, we restrict primary diagnostics to features with m_eff > 5**,
where the test has sufficient resolution to behave meaningfully.

## Calibration After m_eff > 5 Filter

```{r fig-calib-meff5, fig.cap="Calibration plot restricted to features with m_eff > 5. All methods move substantially closer to the nominal diagonal.", out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(t1_meff_dir, "calibration_plot.png"))
```

```{r fig-t1-iter-meff5, fig.cap="Per-iteration type-1 error rate restricted to features with m_eff > 5.", out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(t1_meff_dir, "type1_rate_by_iter.png"))
```

```{r tab-t1-meff5}
t1m_stat %>%
  mutate(
    Method            = stat_labels[aggregate_stat_used],
    `Type-1 (α=0.05)` = sprintf("%.1f%%", mean_type1_0.05 * 100),
    `Type-1 (α=0.01)` = sprintf("%.1f%%", mean_type1_0.01 * 100),
    `λ_GC`            = sprintf("%.2f",   mean_lambda_gc)
  ) %>%
  arrange(match(aggregate_stat_used, stat_order)) %>%
  select(Method, `Type-1 (α=0.05)`, `Type-1 (α=0.01)`, `λ_GC`) %>%
  kable(
    align   = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
    caption = "Empirical type-1 error rates restricted to features with m_eff > 5. AF achieves the best balance: close to nominal 5% without exceeding it."
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

After filtering:

- **AF (2.9%)** is closest to the nominal 5% level while remaining consistently
  conservative, with a well-behaved λ_GC of 1.38.
- **Stouffer (2.8%)** is nearly identical to AF in overall rate and has λ_GC ≈ 1.0,
  but gives up ~2 percentage points of nominal level, which translates to
  reduced power (see Section 3).
- **Maxmean (2.5%)** is the most conservative, with clearly deflated λ_GC < 1.
- **CCT (4.9%)** appears near-nominal in aggregate, but this masks a severe
  structural problem: it becomes increasingly anti-conservative as m_eff
  increases (Table 3).

```{r tab-meffbin-meff5}
cct_rates <- t1m_meffbin %>%
  filter(aggregate_stat_used == "cct") %>%
  arrange(m_eff_bin) %>%
  pull(pooled_rate)

t1m_meffbin %>%
  filter(aggregate_stat_used != "cct") %>%
  bind_rows(t1m_meffbin %>% filter(aggregate_stat_used == "cct")) %>%
  mutate(
    Method = stat_labels[aggregate_stat_used],
    Rate   = sprintf("%.1f%%", pooled_rate * 100),
    `λ_GC` = sprintf("%.2f", lambda_gc)
  ) %>%
  arrange(m_eff_bin, match(aggregate_stat_used, stat_order)) %>%
  select(m_eff_bin, Method, Rate, `λ_GC`) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = Method,
    values_from = c(Rate, `λ_GC`),
    names_glue  = "{Method} {.value}"
  ) %>%
  select(
    m_eff_bin,
    `Stouffer Rate`, `Stouffer λ_GC`,
    `AF Rate`,       `AF λ_GC`,
    `Maxmean Rate`,  `Maxmean λ_GC`,
    `CCT Rate`,      `CCT λ_GC`
  ) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "m_eff bin",
      "Rate", "λ_GC", "Rate", "λ_GC",
      "Rate", "λ_GC", "Rate", "λ_GC"
    ),
    align   = c("l", rep("r", 8)),
    caption = "Type-1 error rate and λ_GC by m_eff bin, restricted to m_eff > 5. CCT (highlighted) becomes anti-conservative above m_eff ≈ 11 and reaches 11.7% at m_eff 251–500. Nominal level: 5%."
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("condensed"), full_width = FALSE, font_size = 12) %>%
  add_header_above(
    c(" " = 1, "Stouffer" = 2, "AF" = 2, "Maxmean" = 2, "CCT" = 2),
    bold = TRUE
  ) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(
    8,
    color = ifelse(cct_rates > ALPHA, "red", "black")
  )
```

The breakdown by m_eff bin reveals that CCT's apparent near-nominal overall
rate is a coincidence: it is deeply conservative at low m_eff and increasingly
anti-conservative at high m_eff, with the two errors cancelling in the
aggregate. At features with more than 25 effective peptides, CCT systematically
exceeds the 5% threshold. AF, Stouffer, and Maxmean all remain below the
nominal level across every m_eff bin.

# Power Analysis

## Effect Templates

The power study evaluated six effect templates derived from real experimental
comparisons. Each template specifies the estimated prevalence of a positive
response in group 1 (prop1) and group 2 (prop2) for each peptide. Simulated
data were generated by drawing binary responses for each subject-peptide pair
from these prevalences.

```{r fig-effects, fig.cap="Peptide-level prevalence in group 1 vs group 2 for each of the six effect templates. The dashed diagonal represents equal prevalence. Colour encodes the signed difference Δ = prop2 − prop1.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(pow_dir, "effect_scatterplots.png"))
```

```{r tab-templates-stats}
tmpl_effects %>%
  mutate(
    Template     = template,
    Feature      = sub("humanbeta5", "hbeta5", sub("Staphylococcus", "S.", feature)),
    Peptides     = n_peptides_total,
    `Mean delta` = sprintf("%+.3f", mean_delta),
    `Max delta`  = sprintf("%.3f",  max_abs_delta),
    `Prev G1`    = sprintf("%.3f",  mean_prop1),
    `Prev G2`    = sprintf("%.3f",  mean_prop2),
    `Pep. aff.`  = sprintf("%.0f%%", frac_diff_sign * 100)
  ) %>%
  arrange(template) %>%
  select(Template, Feature, Peptides,
         `Mean delta`, `Max delta`, `Prev G1`, `Prev G2`, `Pep. aff.`) %>%
  kable(
    align   = c("l","l","r","r","r","r","r","r"),
    caption = "Quantitative summary of the six effect templates. Pep. aff.: fraction of peptides with any non-zero difference."
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

```{r tab-templates-char}
tibble(
  Template  = paste0("effect_", LETTERS[1:6]),
  Feature   = c("Enterovirus", "Bos taurus", "Bubalus bubalis",
                "CMV hbeta5", "S. aureus", "S. aureus (large)"),
  Character = c(
    "Strong, diffuse. Broad downregulation across 93% of 274 peptides.",
    "Moderate, subset-driven. A few peptides carry most of the signal (max single-peptide effect = 0.35).",
    "Strong, concentrated. All 15 peptides are affected; clean uniform upregulation.",
    "Moderate-small, diffuse. Broad downregulation spread across 153 peptides.",
    "Small, diffuse. Consistent downregulation across all 351 peptides.",
    "Very small, very diffuse. All 1103 peptides shift slightly (mean absolute effect = 0.010)."
  )
) %>%
  kable(
    align   = c("l","l","l"),
    caption = "Qualitative characterisation of the six effect templates."
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "20em")
```

The templates span a biologically meaningful range:

- **Effects A, D, E, F** are *diffuse*: the signal is spread across many
  peptides, each contributing a small shift. For effect F (S. aureus, 1,103
  peptides), the mean difference is only +0.010 — essentially every peptide
  shifts slightly, but individually the change is nearly invisible.
- **Effects B and C** are more *concentrated*: a subset of peptides drives
  the majority of the signal (effect B has a maximum peptide-level effect of
  0.35), while the rest contribute modestly.

> **Note on CCT.** Given CCT's anti-conservative type-1 error at high m_eff
> and near-zero power across virtually all scenarios tested, it is excluded
> from the power comparison figures below.

## Power Heatmaps

The heatmaps below show the estimated power (proportion of simulations
correctly detecting the effect at α = 0.05) across the full grid of sample
sizes and peptide counts, separately for each method and effect template. The
80% power threshold is annotated in each cell.

```{r fig-heat-stouffer, fig.cap="Power heatmap — Stouffer method. Each cell shows estimated power at a given combination of sample size (x-axis) and peptide count (y-axis).", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(pow_dir, "power_heatmap_stouffer.png"))
```

```{r fig-heat-af, fig.cap="Power heatmap — AF method.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(pow_dir, "power_heatmap_af.png"))
```

```{r fig-heat-maxmean, fig.cap="Power heatmap — Maxmean method.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(pow_dir, "power_heatmap_maxmean.png"))
```

Several patterns are immediately visible:

1. **Stouffer achieves 80% power at the smallest sample sizes across almost all
   templates**, often at n = 15 even for difficult scenarios such as effect D
   (CMV, mean Δ = −0.047). AF closely mirrors Stouffer for strong and moderate
   effects, with a small gap visible for the weakest template (effect F).

2. **Maxmean performs competitively on concentrated effects** (B and C): it
   reaches 80% power by n = 15–30. However, its performance collapses on diffuse
   effects — it achieves only 1.3% power at n = 15 for effect D and needs
   n = 100 to reach 80%.

3. **The peptide count has a strong positive effect on power for Stouffer and
   AF**, particularly for the weakest effects (E, F). For maxmean, adding
   peptides helps much less on diffuse effects.

## Power vs Sample Size

```{r fig-power-n, fig.cap="Power as a function of subjects per group, at the maximum available peptide count for each template. The dashed horizontal line marks 80% power.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(pow_dir, "power_vs_n_by_stat.png"))
```

For diffuse effects (D, E, F), Stouffer and AF reach the 80% threshold at
n = 15, while maxmean requires far more subjects. For strong, concentrated
effects (A, B, C), all three methods converge quickly.

## Power vs Number of Peptides

```{r fig-power-pep, fig.cap="Power as a function of peptide count, at n = 60 subjects per group. For Stouffer and AF, power increases consistently with peptide count.", out.width="100%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(pow_dir, "power_vs_npep_by_stat.png"))
```

For **Stouffer and AF**, each additional peptide brings new independent evidence
that adds to the aggregate signal — power climbs steeply with peptide count.
For **Maxmean**, the curve is flatter for diffuse effects: selecting only the
single most extreme peptide mean does not accumulate evidence from additional
peptides.

## Minimum Sample Size for 80% Power

```{r tab-n80}
max_pep_per_tmpl <- pow_summary %>%
  group_by(template) %>%
  summarise(max_pep = max(n_peptides_cfg), .groups = "drop")

n80 %>%
  left_join(max_pep_per_tmpl, by = "template") %>%
  filter(n_peptides_cfg == max_pep) %>%
  filter(aggregate_stat_cfg %in% c("stouffer", "af", "maxmean")) %>%
  left_join(tmpl_effects %>% select(template, feature, mean_delta), by = "template") %>%
  mutate(
    n_for_80_label = ifelse(is.na(n_for_80), ">400", as.character(as.integer(n_for_80))),
    Method = stat_labels[aggregate_stat_cfg]
  ) %>%
  select(template, feature, mean_delta, Method, n_for_80_label) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Method, values_from = n_for_80_label) %>%
  arrange(template) %>%
  mutate(
    Template = template,
    Feature  = feature,
    `Mean Δ` = sprintf("%+.3f", mean_delta)
  ) %>%
  select(Template, Feature, `Mean Δ`, Stouffer, AF, Maxmean) %>%
  kable(
    align   = c("l","l","r","r","r","r"),
    caption = "Minimum subjects per group required to achieve 80% power (at maximum available peptide count). '>400' means 80% was not achieved within the evaluated range."
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

For virtually every template, **Stouffer and AF require the same minimum sample
size**. The one exception is effect F (mean Δ = +0.010), where Stouffer achieves
80% power at n = 15 while AF requires n = 30. Maxmean requires 2–6× more
subjects for diffuse effects.

---

# Summary and Recommendations

## Overall Performance Summary

```{r tab-global-power}
grid_stats <- pow_summary %>%
  filter(aggregate_stat_cfg %in% c("stouffer","af","maxmean")) %>%
  group_by(aggregate_stat_cfg) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_power = mean(power),
    pct_ge80   = mean(power >= 0.80),
    pct_ge90   = mean(power >= 0.90),
    pct_ge95   = mean(power >= 0.95),
    .groups    = "drop"
  )

t1_meff_clean <- t1m_stat %>%
  filter(aggregate_stat_used %in% c("stouffer","af","maxmean")) %>%
  select(aggregate_stat_used, mean_type1_0.05, mean_lambda_gc) %>%
  rename(aggregate_stat_cfg = aggregate_stat_used)

left_join(grid_stats, t1_meff_clean, by = "aggregate_stat_cfg") %>%
  mutate(
    Method              = stat_labels[aggregate_stat_cfg],
    `Mean power`        = sprintf("%.3f", mean_power),
    `≥80% of cells`     = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_ge80 * 100),
    `≥90% of cells`     = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_ge90 * 100),
    `Type-1 (m_eff>5)`  = sprintf("%.1f%%", mean_type1_0.05 * 100),
    `λ_GC (m_eff>5)`    = sprintf("%.2f",   mean_lambda_gc)
  ) %>%
  arrange(match(aggregate_stat_cfg, c("stouffer","af","maxmean"))) %>%
  select(Method, `Mean power`, `≥80% of cells`, `≥90% of cells`,
         `Type-1 (m_eff>5)`, `λ_GC (m_eff>5)`) %>%
  kable(
    align   = c("l","r","r","r","r","r"),
    caption = "Overall performance summary. Power statistics are computed across all 156 grid cells (6 templates × n × peptide combinations). Type-1 error and λ_GC are from the m_eff > 5 filtered analysis."
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

## Conclusions

**1. CCT should not be used in this setting.** Its power is negligible (mean
power 5.7%), and it becomes anti-conservative for features with more than ~10
effective peptides. This is a structural incompatibility, not a tunable
parameter.

**2. Stouffer is the most powerful method overall.** It achieves 80% power in
75.6% of all evaluated scenarios, compared to 71.2% for AF and 48.1% for
maxmean. Its advantage is most pronounced for diffuse effects — the biologically
common scenario where the immune response is spread across many peptides.

**3. Maxmean should be reserved for concentrated effects.** It is competitive
with Stouffer and AF when the signal is carried by a few strong peptides
(templates B and C), but fails severely on diffuse effects — requiring 4–6×
more subjects to achieve the same power as Stouffer.

**4. AF is the best all-round choice when calibration is a priority.** It is
the closest to the nominal 5% type-1 error rate (2.9% at m_eff > 5) without
ever exceeding it, and its power deficit relative to Stouffer is typically 0–3
percentage points, recoverable with a modest increase in sample size.

## Practical Recommendations

| Scenario | Recommended method | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Default analysis, exploratory | **AF** | Best calibration, high power, safe across m_eff range |
| Sample size is binding constraint | **Stouffer** | Maximum power at any given n; especially for diffuse effects |
| Known concentrated epitope target | **Maxmean** | Competitive power when few peptides drive the signal |
| Any setting | **Avoid CCT** | Anti-conservative at high m_eff; near-zero power |
| All analyses | **Apply m_eff > 5 filter** | Removes pathologically conservative low-peptide features |

The m_eff > 5 filter deserves particular emphasis: it is not a post-hoc
correction, but a principled exclusion of features for which the permutation
test lacks sufficient resolution to produce informative p-values. Applying this
filter before interpreting results is recommended regardless of which
aggregation method is used.
